title: Risk, Vulnerabilities & Security Frameworks
summary: The precise vocabulary — vulnerability, threat, risk, exploit — plus CVSS, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and where compliance fits, all at interview depth rather than audit-checklist depth.

slides.markdown:
Security has its own precise vocabulary, and interviewers use it as a filter: mixing up **vulnerability**, **threat**, **risk**, and **exploit** in the same sentence is a fast signal of surface-level knowledge.

This topic locks down those definitions, then covers the two pieces of scaffolding built on top of them: **CVSS**, the standard for scoring how severe a specific vulnerability is, and the **NIST Cybersecurity Framework**, the standard for organizing a security program's activities end to end. It closes with where compliance (SOC2, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS) actually fits relative to engineering security work — a distinction that trips up even experienced engineers.

This closes out Security Fundamentals: everything here — CIA, design principles, defense in depth, threat modeling — feeds into the risk-scoring and prioritization vocabulary this topic gives a name to.

slides.subTitle: Precise definitions
slides.markdown:
Four terms, used loosely in everyday speech and precisely in security work — and the precision matters because each implies a different response:

- **Vulnerability** — a weakness in a system: an unpatched library, a missing input check, a misconfigured permission. It exists whether or not anyone is currently attacking it.
- **Threat** — a potential source of harm that could exploit a vulnerability: a specific attacker group, a piece of malware, an insider. A threat needs a vulnerability (or a target) to act against; a vulnerability can exist with no threat currently pursuing it.
- **Exploit** — the actual code, technique, or method that takes advantage of a vulnerability. A vulnerability can exist for years with no public exploit, which is a large part of why "vulnerable" doesn't automatically mean "actively dangerous."
- **Risk** — the combination of all three: the likelihood a threat exploits a vulnerability, multiplied by the impact if it does. Risk is what you actually manage; vulnerabilities and threats are inputs to that calculation.

Saying "this vulnerability is a risk" without naming a threat and an impact is an incomplete sentence — it's the equivalent of quoting Big-O without saying what n counts.

The **Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS)** converts a vulnerability's characteristics into a standardized 0–10 severity score, so vulnerabilities from different vendors and tools can be compared on the same scale.

The score is built from metrics grouped into a few categories: **attack vector** (does it require network access, or physical presence at the machine?), **attack complexity** (does it need special conditions, or does it work reliably every time?), **privileges required** (none, or an existing account?), **user interaction** (does a victim have to click something?), and the **impact** on confidentiality, integrity, and availability if exploited.

A vulnerability exploitable over the network, with no privileges and no user interaction required, and full impact on all three CIA properties, scores near 10 — a remote code execution flaw in an internet-facing service is the canonical example. A vulnerability requiring local physical access and already-elevated privileges, with minor impact, scores much lower even if it's conceptually the same *class* of bug.

A CVSS score is derived from a compact **vector string** that a security engineer should be able to skim, not just the final number:

```text
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
```

| Metric | Value here | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| AV (Attack Vector) | N (Network) | Exploitable remotely, no local access needed |
| AC (Attack Complexity) | L (Low) | No special conditions required |
| PR (Privileges Required) | N (None) | No account needed to exploit |
| UI (User Interaction) | N (None) | No victim click needed |
| C/I/A Impact | H/H/H | High impact on all three CIA properties |

This is a worst-case profile — remotely exploitable, trivial, no privileges, no interaction, full impact — and it's exactly why a bug like this (an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw) scores near the top of the scale. Reading the vector string tells you *why* a score is what it is, which matters because two 9.8-scoring bugs with different vectors can call for different urgency depending on what's actually reachable in your environment.

slides.sectionTitle: NIST Cybersecurity Framework, at a glance
slides.markdown:
Where CVSS scores a single vulnerability, the **NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)** organizes an entire security program's activities into five functions, meant to run continuously and in parallel, not as sequential phases:

- **Identify** — know your assets, data, and risk exposure (you can't protect what you haven't inventoried).
- **Protect** — the controls this whole area teaches: access control, encryption, training, secure design.
- **Detect** — logging, monitoring, and anomaly detection to notice when protection fails.
- **Respond** — incident response: contain, eradicate, communicate.
- **Recover** — restore normal operation and feed lessons learned back into Identify.

The framework's real value for an engineer isn't memorizing the five words — it's the diagnostic use: if an organization only has strong **Protect** controls and nothing for **Detect**, an attacker who gets past prevention operates undetected indefinitely. Most "why didn't we notice this sooner" postmortems trace back to a gap in Detect or Respond, not Protect — a program can be excellent at building walls and still fail badly at noticing when one's been climbed.

**Compliance frameworks** — SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS — certify that an organization follows a defined set of controls and processes, usually verified by an external auditor on a fixed schedule (annually, typically). **Engineering security work** is the ongoing practice of actually finding and fixing weaknesses: threat modeling, code review, patching, monitoring.

The relationship between them is easy to get backwards. Compliance is a **floor and a snapshot**, not a security guarantee — passing a SOC 2 audit proves you had the required controls in place *at the time of the audit*, not that you're secure today or that the controls are effective against a real attacker. Plenty of breached companies were compliant with the relevant framework at the time of their breach; compliance and security are correlated but not identical.

The common engineering mistake is treating compliance requirements as the actual security target ("we need MFA because PCI-DSS requires it") instead of understanding *why* the control exists ("MFA because a stolen password shouldn't be enough to access payment systems") — the second framing generalizes to new situations the compliance checklist didn't anticipate; the first doesn't.

The framing that ties this whole group together: security isn't a project with a completion date, it's an ongoing process that has to keep pace with a system that never stops changing.

Every input to the risk calculation shifts constantly and independently: new code ships with new vulnerabilities, new CVEs get published against dependencies you already run, attacker techniques evolve (a technique considered exotic five years ago is now automated and commodified), and your own system's architecture changes as it grows. A risk assessment, a threat model, or a CVSS score is a snapshot of one moment — accurate when written, decaying from the moment it's filed.

This is why mature security programs build recurring cadences into the calendar rather than treating any single review as final: periodic dependency scanning (not a one-time audit), scheduled threat-model revisits tied to architecture changes, continuous monitoring rather than point-in-time log reviews. The NIST CSF's five functions being circular rather than linear — Recover feeds back into Identify — is the same idea formalized: there's no final step.

slides.sectionTitle: High CVSS, low exposure vs medium CVSS, trivial exploit
slides.markdown:
| | High-CVSS bug, no real exposure | Medium-CVSS bug, trivially exploitable |
|---|---|---|
| **Example** | 9.8 remote code execution in a library, but the vulnerable function is never called and the service isn't internet-facing | 5.3 information disclosure that leaks a session token via a URL a link-preview bot follows automatically |
| **CVSS score** | Very high on paper | Moderate on paper |
| **Real-world likelihood** | Effectively zero — nothing reaches the vulnerable code path | High — the trigger condition happens automatically, constantly |
| **Actual priority** | Low, once exposure is confirmed | High — should likely be fixed first |

This is the single most important nuance in vulnerability management: **CVSS scores severity in a vacuum, not risk in your specific environment.** The score doesn't know whether the vulnerable code path is reachable, whether the service is internet-facing, or whether an existing compensating control (a WAF rule, network segmentation) already blocks the path. Two teams with the same CVE can have wildly different actual risk, and treating the raw score as the priority ranking without checking exposure is how the wrong bug gets fixed first.

A concrete version of the previous slide's comparison, as an actual triage call a security team might make on the same Monday morning:

- **Finding A**: a CVSS 9.8 in a JSON parsing library used transitively by a background reporting job that runs in an isolated network with no internet access and no untrusted input. Exploitability in this specific deployment: effectively none.
- **Finding B**: a CVSS 6.1 cross-site scripting bug in a customer-facing support portal that any unauthenticated user can trigger by submitting a crafted support ticket, viewed by every agent who opens it.

A CVSS-score-only triage fixes A first and queues B for "next sprint." A risk-aware triage fixes B today — it's live, exploitable by anyone right now, and hits real users and staff — and schedules A for the next routine dependency bump, since its actual likelihood in this environment is near zero.

This is what "security engineering judgment" concretely means in a vulnerability management role: the score is an input to the decision, not the decision itself.

slides.sectionTitle: Chasing the CVSS number instead of exploitability
slides.markdown:
The pitfall the previous three slides built toward, stated directly: optimizing a vulnerability-management program around the raw CVSS score, rather than actual exploitability in your specific environment.

This happens for an understandable reason — a single number is easy to report up the chain ("we closed all criticals this quarter") and easy to set an SLA against. But CVSS is explicitly designed to score a vulnerability in the abstract, not to predict what happens in your deployment. A program that patches every 9+ on a fixed SLA regardless of reachability will burn its scarcest resource — engineering time — on bugs that were never actually exploitable, while a lower-scored but live, reachable bug waits in the backlog.

The fix is layering an **exposure and reachability check** on top of the raw score before prioritizing: is the vulnerable code path actually invoked, is the service actually reachable by an untrusted party, is there already a compensating control. Several organizations now track this as a separate score (sometimes called "exploit prediction" or environmental context) precisely because raw CVSS alone reliably misprioritizes a meaningful fraction of real backlogs.

This closes the group, and the vocabulary here is what turns everything before it into something you can actually prioritize with. CIA told you *what* to protect. Design principles and defense in depth told you *how* to build resilient controls. Threat modeling told you *how to find* specific weaknesses in a specific design. This topic tells you how to *score and rank* what you find, and how to see through the difference between a compliance checkbox and an actual reduction in risk.

The single sentence that summarizes the whole group, and that most candidates only get half of in an interview: **security is a continuous process of identifying real risk — likelihood and impact together, in your specific context — and reducing it through layered, well-designed controls**, not a score to hit, a checklist to complete, or a project with an end date.

The next groups in this area — Cryptography, Application Security, and beyond — are the specific technical controls this vocabulary and process get applied to.
